 5.1 Project management, CPM and PERT

 A project is a set of inter-related activities (tasks) that must be carried out in a definite order, with a clear start and finish, to
 reach one goal (e.g. building a plant, launching a product, publishing a book). Network analysis models the project as a
 network of arrows and nodes so that it can be planned, scheduled, monitored and controlled.


 Managers have planned large projects for centuries, but management-science techniques were applied to them only in the
 last ~60 years.

 1957 — CPM (Critical Path Method) was developed by Kelly and Walker (for DuPont) to help build and maintain chemical
 plants.
 1958 — PERT (Program Evaluation and Review Technique) was developed by the Special Projects Office of the US Navy to
 plan and control the Polaris missile programme.

 Both are used to plan the scheduling of individual activities: they give the earliest/latest start and finish of every activity, the
 project completion time and the slack of each activity.

Questions PERT/CPM answer

 1. When will the entire project be completed?

 2. Which are the critical activities — the ones that delay the whole project if they are late?

 3. Which are the non-critical activities — the ones that can run late without delaying completion?

 4. What is the probability that the project will be completed by a specific date? (PERT)

 5. On any date, is the project on schedule, behind schedule or ahead of schedule?

 6. Is the money spent equal to, less than or more than the budget?

 7. Are there enough resources to finish on time?

 8. If the project must be finished sooner, what is the cheapest way to do it? (crash analysis)

 5.2 Network terminology

 Activity — a task or item of work that consumes time, effort, money and other resources. It is drawn as an arrow, the head
 showing the direction of progress. The arrow is not drawn to scale. An activity starting at event i and ending at event j is
 written (i, j), i ≠ j. An activity cannot start until its preceding events have occurred.


 Event (node) — the numbered circle marking the start or end of an activity. It is a specific accomplishment that happens at
 an instant of time, so it does not consume time or resources.

 Dummy activity Shown by a dotted arrow. Used when event j cannot occur until event i has occurred but no real job lies between

Good habits for large networks
 Avoid arrows that cross each other.
 Use straight arrows.

 Do not try to show the duration of an activity by its arrow length.
 Draw arrows from left to right; avoid mixing directions (vertical arrows may be used if needed).

 Use dummies freely in a rough draft, but the final network should have no redundant dummies.
 The network has only one start event and one end event.

Common errors in drawing networks

 Error What goes wrong

 1. Dangling An activity gets disconnected before all activities are complete (it has no successor and is not the end). It breaks the
 rule of only one end event.

 2. Looping Because of a faulty sequence an endless loop is formed and the network cannot proceed. Avoid it by checking the
 (cycling) precedence relationships and numbering events in logical order.

 3. Redundancy Presence of an unnecessary dummy activity in the network logic.

 5.4 Fulkerson’s rule
Fulkerson’s rule has two parts: the rules for representing activities and the rule for numbering events.

Representation Numbering the nodes
 Every activity is shown by a single arrow.
 1. Number the start event 1.
 Each activity has a unique start node and end node.
 2. Delete (mentally) all arrows leaving event 1. This creates new
 No two activities have the same start and end nodes. “start” events (events with no incoming arrows); number them
 Nodes are events (start/finish points), not tasks. 2, 3, … working left to right / top to bottom.

 Activities that depend on the same event share that node. 3. Repeat: delete the arrows leaving the newly numbered events
 Dummies (dashed arrows) show a dependency without adding and number the next set of events with no remaining incoming
 work or time. arrows.

 In short: arrows = tasks, nodes = events. 4. Continue until the end event is numbered. Every arrow then
 goes from a smaller to a bigger number (i < j); no number is
 repeated.

 5. If two activities would share both nodes, insert a dummy so the
 numbering stays unique.

Steps to find the critical path

 1. Draw the network from the precedence table and number events by Fulkerson’s rule.

 2. Forward pass (left → right): TE of the start event = 0. For every other event, TEj = max(TEi + tij) over all arrows ending at j.
 Then ES = TEi, EF = ES + t. The project time is TE of the finish event (= max EF).

 3. Backward pass (right → left): TL of the finish event = its TE. For every other event, TLi = min(TLj − tij) over all arrows leaving i.
 Then LF = TLj, LS = LF − t.

 4. Floats: TF = LS − ES (= LF − EF). Free float = TEj − EF.

 5.7 PERT — time estimates and probability
The main objective of PERT is to find the chance of completing a particular event (usually the whole project) within a specified
date. It takes the uncertainties of activity times into account by using three time estimates.

 Estimate Meaning

 Optimistic time to (a) Shortest possible time, if everything goes very well.

 Most likely time tm (m) Normal time, assuming normal delays; the time with the highest frequency if completion times were plotted.

 Pessimistic time tp (b) Longest time, if everything goes wrong (only about 1 in 100 would take longer).



 Expected time (activity time follows a Beta distribution): te = (to + 4tm + tp) / 6 — the average time if the

 activity were repeated many times.

6.2 Two-person zero-sum games and the pay-off matrix

 A two-person zero-sum (rectangular) game has two players, A and B, and whatever A gains B loses (and vice-versa), so the
 payoffs sum to zero. It is written as an m × n pay-off matrix: rows = A’s m strategies, columns = B’s n strategies, entry aij =
 payoff to A (the maximiser, on the left) when A plays i and B plays j. A negative entry is a gain to B.


 Convention. The player on the left (rows) is the maximising player; the player on top (columns) is the minimising player. If
 the matrix is given from the perspective of the column player (for example “pay-off matrix for firm A” in the exam, or costs
 to a company), read carefully who maximises.

Value of the game, maximin and minimax
 Value of the game (V) — the expected outcome when both players follow their optimal strategies.
 Maximin criterion (A, maximiser) — list the minimum of each row, then select the strategy with the maximum of these
 minima (A’s guaranteed gain).

 Minimax criterion (B, minimiser) — list the maximum of each column, then select the strategy with the minimum of these
 maxima (B’s limit on loss).
 Always: maximin ≤ V ≤ minimax.


 Saddle point — if maximin = minimax, the game has a saddle (equilibrium) point. The entry is the minimum of its row and
 the maximum of its column (the shape of a saddle). The strategies there are the optimal strategies and the entry is the
 value of the game.


 A game may have more than one saddle point (all with the same value); some games have none.

 Strictly determinable game — maximin value = minimax value; a saddle point exists and the game is solved by pure
 strategies.
 Fair game — value of the game is zero: neither player gains or loses in the long run.

 Perfect/imperfect, zero-sum — see 6.1.

Procedure to find a saddle point

 1. Row minima — write the smallest element of each row; pick the largest of them (maximin) and enclose it in a rectangle.

 2. Column maxima — write the largest element of each column; pick the smallest of them (minimax) and enclose it in a circle.

 7.1 Simulation — introduction

 Simulation is a technique of performing experiments on a mathematical model that represents a real-life system, to study
 how the system behaves under different conditions (Hira & Gupta). Instead of solving equations, we imitate the system on
 paper or on a computer and read the answers from the results.


When is simulation used?
 The system is too complex for an analytical (closed-form) solution.
 Randomness / uncertainty plays a major role (random demand, arrival and service times, breakdowns).

 Experimenting on the real system is costly, risky or impossible (“what-if” analysis without disturbing operations).

 Typical OR applications: queuing and service systems, inventory control, production scheduling, project networks.

Steps in a simulation study

 1. Problem definition — identify the system, the objectives and the performance measures.

 2. Model formulation — define the system variables and their inter-relationships.

 3. Data collection — gather statistical data for the probabilistic inputs (e.g. demand distribution).

 4. Model translation (coding) — convert the logical model into a simulation language / spreadsheet / program.

 5. Verification and validation — is the model built right, and does it behave like the real system?

 6. Experimental design — choose the alternatives to compare and the number of runs.

 7. Output analysis — summarise and interpret the results statistically.

 8. Implementation — apply the findings to the real system.

Advantages and limitations

 7.3 Monte Carlo simulation

 Monte Carlo simulation estimates the behaviour of a system with random inputs by repeatedly drawing random numbers,
 converting them into values of the random variable through its probability distribution, and averaging the outcomes.


Procedure

 1. Check that the probabilities of the distribution add up to 1.

 2. Compute the cumulative probability column.

 3. Assign random-number intervals (00–99 for two digits): each value gets as many numbers as 100 × its probability, in order,
 starting from 00. The interval of a value runs from the previous cumulative × 100 up to its own cumulative × 100 − 1.

 4. For each trial take the next random number and find the interval it falls in; read off the value (demand, time, …).

 5. Tabulate and compute the required average / total / count. Compare with the theoretical expected value E(X) = Σ x·p.

 7.6 Two machines, n jobs — Johnson’s rule

 Johnson’s rule is a procedure that gives the sequence of n jobs on two machines (all jobs go M1 then M2) with the
 minimum total elapsed time, which also minimises the total idle time of the machines.




Unit 7 · Simulation and Sequencing Made by Jay Naik Page 70 of 84

Conditions
 Job times are known and constant, and independent of the sequence.
 Every job passes through the same two machines in the same order (M1 first, then M2).

 Job priorities cannot be used.
 A job is available on M2 only after it has finished on M1; each machine processes one job at a time.

Steps

 1. Find the shortest processing time among the jobs not yet scheduled (on both machines). Ties: choose any one.

 2. If it is on Machine 1, place that job as early as possible (next free position from the front). If it is on Machine 2, place that
 job as late as possible (next free position from the back).

 3. Remove the job scheduled; repeat steps 1–2 for the remaining jobs until all are placed.

 4. Build the schedule: M1 works without a break; a job starts on M2 at max(its finish on M1, finish of the previous job on M2).
 Total elapsed time = finish of the last job on M2.


 Remember: Idle time. Idle time of M1 = total elapsed time − ΣM1 times (it waits at the end). Idle time of M2 = waiting
 before its first job (= M1 time of the first job) + all gaps between jobs on M2. Equivalent check: ΣM2 times + idle(M2) =
 total elapsed time.

 7.8 n jobs on m machines
 With n jobs and m machines in a fixed order, a permutation schedule (same job order on every machine) is chosen from n!
 orders; allowing different orders on different machines gives (n!)m schedules — far too many to enumerate.

 There is no simple exact rule like Johnson’s for m ≥ 4 in general; the problem is solved by exact methods (branch and bound,
 integer programming) for small cases and by heuristics for large ones.
 If the two-machine style conditions hold (the middle machines are never the bottleneck: min A ≥ max of every middle
 machine, or min of the last machine ≥ max of every middle machine) the problem reduces to two fictitious machines: A′ =
 sum of the first m−1 machines, B′ = sum of the last m−1 machines. Apply Johnson’s rule to (A′, B′).

 Campbell–Dudek–Smith (CDS) heuristic (when the condition fails): for k = 1 … m−1 form A(k) = sum of the first k machines
 and B(k) = sum of the last k machines, apply Johnson’s rule, evaluate each sequence on the real machines, and keep the
 best of the m−1 sequences.

 Term / rule One-line meaning

 CPM Deterministic network method (Kelly & Walker, 1957); one time estimate; finds critical path and
 crash plan.

 Network rules One start and one end event; one arrow per activity; no two activities with same head and tail;

 Fulkerson’s rule Number start event 1; delete its arrows; number new start events left→right; repeat; every arrow
